pr_body:
Changes the `VariantUtility` function from `print_verbose` to `_print_verbose`, eliminating the need for undefining the `print_verbose` macro, which caused compilation problems.

Fixes #101966

## Notes
* Although the problem was seen occurring in a SCU build, the problem was not directly related to SCU, but rather the fact that `variant_utility.h` undefined `print_verbose`.
* This meant that any code compiled _after_ this include would fail to compile `print_verbose`.
* Feel free to suggest any variations on the macro name / func name, these were just a quick guess.

## Discussion
`VariantUtility` contained a `print_verbose` function for binding (with gdscript etc) which conflicted with the global definition of `print_verbose`. This had been worked around by undefining `print_verbose` in these files, which was a little hacky, and had the side effect of breaking compilation in any later file that tried to use `print_verbose`.

The more sensible solution was to give the `VariantUtility` function a different name. @Calinou informed me that it was possible to bind a function with a different name exposed to gdscript than the c++ function, and this (hopefully) provides the simplest solution.

Please target the `master` branch in priority.

pr_comments:
Yup a templated function was my first thought too, however I was suspecting the reason for using a define was to try and remove the work of the string concatenation:

For instance
```
print_verbose("blah blah" + "blah" + itos(a));
```
With a templated function, will it do the concatenation work, even though it will not be used further on? Or does the variable  args remove this problem?

With the define, if the `is_print_verbose_enabled()` fails, it should avoid the string concatenation.

There is a note about this in the source:
```
// This version avoids processing the text to be printed until it actually has to be printed, saving some CPU usage.
#define print_verbose(m_text)             \
	{                                     \
		if (is_print_verbose_enabled()) { \
			print_line(m_text);           \
		}                                 \
	}
```

Right. That makes sense, I suppose.
Then I would say the best solution would be a full project find and replace of `print_verbose` -> `PRINT_VERBOSE`. The reason macros are usually uppercase is precisely to avoid this kind of issue, where it interferes with normal function usage.

I do agree on capitalization for macros, mind you that approach might be subject to more push back (as the change is less localized), and will require rebasing existing PRs that use `print_verbose`.

I wouldn't be surprised if this was historically a function and later changed to a macro for the string concat efficiency.

Probably better for a separate PR though, so preferred approach can be chosen in a meeting.

> Then I would say the best solution would be a full project find and replace of `print_verbose` -> `PRINT_VERBOSE`. The reason macros are usually uppercase is precisely to avoid this kind of issue, where it interferes with normal function usage.

There is already a PR to do exactly that: #100224.

But indeed, as I commented there, `print_verbose` is meant to look and feel like a function because it's similar to the `print_line` and `print_error` functions.

But its argument can often be costly to compute, hence why it was made a macro to avoid paying that cost. That makes it possible to use `print_verbose` relatively liberally without worrying too much that this will have a performance impact in production builds.

Whether that's a premature optimization, this would likely be worth testing.
Realized it would be better to call this new macro from FUNCBINDVARARGV, to reduce the code duplication and make it clearer, have re-pushed, should be clearer now what is going on.

> Whether that's a premature optimization, this would likely be worth testing.

The macro approach is definitely worth doing - I was doing some profiling a couple of days ago with a similar logging macro, and the cost of concatenating strings that will never be printed is indeed significant.
When I brought up premature optimization i failed to consider that the argument evaluation could be deferred; i thought it may only try to avoid a call. It being a macro makes more sense to me now!

issue_context.title: `print_verbose` makes build fail when `scu_build=yes`
issue_context.body:
### Tested versions

- 4.4.beta

### System information

Windows 11

### Issue description

The `print_verbose` macro is causing one of the CI jobs that uses `scu_build=yes` to fail in my PR although I didn't modify the file calling it.
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/actions/runs/12934119444/job/36074414239

My local build also fails when I use `scu_build=yes` but works fine otherwise.
```sh
[100%] godot\core/debugger/remote_debugger_peer.cpp(172): error C3861: 'print_verbose': identifier not found
```

By the way, it works if I replace it with `WARN_VERBOSE`.

### Steps to reproduce

- Checkout https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/100516
- I changed calls to `print_verbose`  in `core/debugger/remote_debugger_peer.cpp` to `WARN_VERBOSE` to fix CI. Change it back to `print_verbose`. 
- Build it with `scons scu_build=yes`.

### Minimal reproduction project (MRP)

N/A
comments:
I can confirm that cherry-picking the mentioned pr and trying to compile with `scu_build=yes` in MSVC 14.3 results in the error (i cherry-picked before the change in the pr that replace the `print_verbose` for `WARN_VERBOSE`)

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/784c5a90-6d12-444c-a35d-05834addb85f)

The problem is likely due to this, in `variant_utility.cpp` and `variant_utility.h`:
```
#undef print_verbose
```
This means anything that tries to use `print_verbose` after these files will fail (unless it is defined after this point).

We can't do much about the header, but for the cpp, we can add it as an exception from the scu build so it gets compiled on its own and doesn't affect any other files.

It likely wasn't due to your PR, but your PR may have inadvertently changed the grouping of which files were compiled together, which exposed this bug.

I'll see if it can be fixed with a simple exception rule.

### UPDATE
The gravy thickens:
```
    process_folder(["core/variant"], ["variant_utility"])
```
It is already added as an exception in the SCU build, so the problem may be the header, and inclusion order. This may be a gotcha of the header (and if so could theoretically also occur in non-scu build). I'll see if there is a sensible fix.

I *think* that `VariantUtility` is providing it's own version of `print_verbose` (instead of the define) so the function can be bound and used by gdscript using the same name.

The problem the `#undef` causes is that any file that includes `variant_utility.h` can no longer use `print_verbose` from c++ _unless_ it includes `core/string/print_string.h` _after_ variant utility. Unfortunately the `clangformat` step re-orders includes, so could inadvertently cause this problem. 🤔 

Yes I confirmed the hypothesis.
Adding:
```
#ifndef print_verbose
#define print_verbose(m_text)             \
{                                     \
			if (is_print_verbose_enabled()) { \
				print_line(m_text);           \
	}                                 \
}
#endif
```
Into `remote_debugger_peer.cpp` solves the problem (although isn't a good proper fix).

Essentially this happens:
* `print_string.h` is included (defining print_verbose)
* Someone includes `variant_utility.h` (undefining it)
* At this stage reincluding `print_string.h` doesn't work as the include guards prevent it running a second time, and `print_verbose` remains undefined.

review_comments: push_back in a loop :s . Would be better to resize + direct assignment, to ensure only one allocation.

Agreed, but this is copied as is from `FUNCBINDVARARGV` (the only change is the c++ function name), so any improvements to efficiency here is out of scope.

Actually looking at it, it might be better to call this new macro from `FUNCBINDVARARGV`, to reduce the code duplication and make it clearer, so I'll change this.
